world.title: Health Sovereignty, Financing Reform and Protecting What Matters Most: Women’s, Children’s and Adolescents’ Health
world.description: The global health landscape is undergoing profound change, with declining development assistance, tightening fiscal space and shifting geopolitical priorities reshaping how health systems are financed and governed. As countries advance health sovereignty agendas and global reform processes accelerate, a critical question emerges: will these transitions protect what matters most, or leave women, children and adolescents behind? Join the Lives in the Balance dialogue on Sunday, 17 May 2026 (18:00–19:30 CET) at the Musée international de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge, where leaders will examine how financing decisions directly impact access to sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) and broader WCAH outcomes. Grounded in the understanding that financing choices are political choices, the session will work to secure recognition of WCAH and SRHR within financing agendas, identify concrete budget protection approaches for country action, and launch the PMNCH financing campaign with a clear follow-up mechanism. Register today to be part of shaping a more equitable global health future.
world.source: PMNCH - Partnership for Maternal, Newborn and Child Health

science.title: Engineering tough blood clots for rapid haemostasis and enhanced regeneration
science.description: Blood clots are pivotal for haemostasis and regeneration1, but they are mechanically weak and form slowly2, posing risks for life-threatening haemorrhage and limiting broader applications3–5. These limitations are attributed to complex coagulation cascades, abundant mechanically ineffective cells and little structural polymers. Strategies that strengthen polymer networks are inapplicable to these highly cellularized materials. Here we report a strategy that rapidly crosslinks red blood cells into tough cytogels and integrates them within blood clots. The resulting engineered blood clots (EBCs) form within seconds and exhibit a 13-fold increase in fracture toughness, and a 4-fold improvement in adhesion energy compared with native clots. Experiments and modelling identify the rupture of mechanically integrated cells as a key toughening mechanism. In vivo studies demonstrate that EBCs can rapidly halt haemorrhage, promote tissue regeneration, mitigate inflammation and foreign body reactions, and prevent postoperative adhesion. The safety and efficacy of both autologous and allogeneic EBCs were also validated. Our strategy is applicable to a range of cells and polymers. This work may motivate the development and translation of highly cellularized materials for bleeding control, wound management, tissue repair and regenerative medicine. Engineered blood clots using rapidly crosslinked red blood cells form within seconds, greatly improving toughness and adhesion while effectively stopping bleeding and enhancing tissue repair.
